summary: This proposed standard defines how DTLS, RTP, RTCP, STUN, TURN and ZRTP packets are multiplexed on a single receiving socket. It overrides guidance in RFC 5764 on the topic, so one port can handle all these kinds of traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: A single mailbox may receive many kinds of mail. This explains how to tell each kind apart so one mailbox can be used for all of them.

questions: multiplex dtls rtp stun on one port
how to multiplex stun dtls and rtp on one port
what is the first byte range for dtls
subtitle: How one UDP port can carry STUN, ZRTP, DTLS, TURN channels and RTP by looking at the first byte.

tldr.problem: RFC 5764 told receivers to sort packets on one port by their first byte, but it silently used up STUN and TLS codepoints and ignored ZRTP and TURN channels.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7983 replaces the sorting rule with a complete table of first-byte ranges (STUN, ZRTP, DTLS, TURN channel, RTP/RTCP) and edits the IANA registries so future allocations cannot collide.
tldr.outcome: Receivers now have an explicit rule for every range, and unknown first bytes must be dropped. The RFC updates RFC 5764 and has itself been updated by RFC 9443.

today: RFC 7983 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2016. It updates RFC 5764 and is itself updated by RFC 9443.

sections.title: Four Problems in RFC 5764
sections.content:
Section 5.1.2 of RFC 5764 lets a receiver demultiplex DTLS, STUN and SRTP/SRTCP packets that arrive on the RTP port. The receiver looks at the first byte of each packet to decide where it goes.

RFC 7983 lists four issues with that scheme:

  • It implicitly allocated codepoints for new STUN methods, with no IANA registry showing it.
  • It did not account for ZRTP, which must also be demultiplexed.
  • It implicitly allocated codepoints for new TLS ContentTypes, again with no registry showing it.
  • It did not account for TURN channels, which also arrive on the same socket.

The overlap between registries means that assigning a value in one protocol can break multiplexing in another, which forces coordination where none should be needed. Because RFC 5764 has been widely deployed, the RFC asks the IANA registry experts to raise a flag when a codepoint would irrevocably prevent multiplexing. It has two goals: make future allocations aware of their impact, and let new protocols join the multiplexed set without breaking existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said which mail goes where, but it forgot some kinds of mail and quietly used up some sticker colours. This RFC fixes the list.

sections.title: Reserving STUN Method Codepoints
sections.content:
RFC 5764 treats a first byte of 0 or 1 as STUN. That restricts STUN method codepoints to 0x000 to 0x07F. The IETF Review range (0x000 to 0x7FF) would shrink from 2048 values to only 128, and the Designated Expert range (0x800 to 0xFFF) would disappear.

To keep the Designated Expert range, RFC 7983 also allocates first-byte values 2 and 3 to STUN. The "STUN Methods" registry is changed so that 0x000 to 0x07F is IETF Review, 0x080 to 0x0FF is Designated Expert, and 0x100 to 0xFFF is Reserved. Reserved codepoints can still be allocated, but only through IETF Review with a document that evaluates the risk of overlapping with other registries.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a few STUN labels fit under the old rule, so this RFC gives STUN a few more sticker numbers and locks the rest away unless careful people agree.

sections.title: ZRTP and TLS ContentTypes
sections.content:
ZRTP is a media-path Diffie-Hellman exchange that agrees on a session key and parameters for unicast SRTP sessions in Voice over IP. It shares the RTP port and needs no support in the signaling protocol. To stop future documents from giving its unused range to a new protocol, RFC 7983 allocates first-byte values 16 to 19 to ZRTP.

For DTLS, a first byte from 20 to 63 means DTLS. For DTLS 1.0 and DTLS 1.2 that byte is the TLS ContentType field. Values 0 to 19 and 64 to 255 therefore need care when new ContentTypes are assigned. The "TLS ContentType Registry" is edited so that 0-19 and 64-255 read "Unassigned (Requires coordination; see RFC 7983)". The assigned values 20 to 24 and the unassigned range 25-63 are unchanged.

RFC 5764 describes a narrow use of DTLS. Any extension or revision to DTLS that no longer meets these first-byte constraints should consider its effect on this multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage: ZRTP gets its own block of sticker numbers. The numbers used by DTLS stay as they were, and the empty numbers around them get a warning sign: ask first.

sections.title: TURN Channels
sections.content:
When used with ICE, an implementation of RFC 5764 can receive packets on one socket from three paths: directly from the source, through a NAT, or relayed by a TURN server. Even after ICE selects a non-relayed path, data can still arrive from the TURN server, for example with aggressive nomination or during an ICE restart.

TURN channels are an optimization that uses a 4-byte prefix instead of the standard 36-byte STUN overhead. Packets over a channel start with a first byte from 64 to 127, which the RFC 5764 scheme would reject. The RFC notes that current implementations violate RFC 5764 for these values and parse them as TURN.

RFC 7983 allocates first-byte values 64 to 79 to TURN channels. This restricts the TURN channel space to a smaller set of possible channels when a client binds a channel while also using this demultiplexing scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail comes through a middleman post office. It was arriving with stickers the old rule did not know, so now it gets a block of numbers of its own.

sections.title: The New Demultiplexing Rule
sections.content:
RFC 7983 replaces the text of Section 5.1.2 of RFC 5764. The receiver looks at the first byte, B:

  • 0 to 3: STUN
  • 16 to 19: ZRTP
  • 20 to 63: DTLS
  • 64 to 79: TURN Channel
  • 128 to 191: RTP (or RTCP, if both are multiplexed over the same destination port)

If the value does not match any known range, the packet MUST be dropped and an alert MAY be logged.
sections.plainLanguage: Look at the first sticker on each packet and send it to the right desk. If the sticker matches no desk, throw the packet away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC updates existing IANA registries and adds a new range for TURN channels in the demultiplexing algorithm. It states that these changes introduce no security considerations beyond those already detailed in RFC 5764.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the sorting list does not open any new doors for troublemakers beyond the ones that were already there.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content: The RFC registers three sets of changes. In the STUN Methods registry, 0x100-0xFFF becomes Reserved and the ranges are reassigned as above. In the TLS ContentType registry, values 0-19 and 64-255 are marked "Unassigned (Requires coordination; see RFC 7983)". In the TURN Channel Numbers registry, 0x5000-0xFFFF is Reserved for DTLS-SRTP multiplexing collision avoidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers is updated so that nobody hands out a reserved number by accident.
